title: Conversion (CCC 1427–1433)
hook: conversion is a lifelong turning of the heart

segments.voice: Yesterday, the fruits of Communion: union, separation from sin, one body, and the poor. Your line was communion makes communion. Did you give the gift you chose? Day one thousand one hundred one.

A courtyard at night, a fire, a servant girl staring. Peter has said it three times now: he doesn't know the man. Somewhere a cock crows. And then comes a line in Luke's Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims, so short it's easy to read past: "And the Lord turning looked on Peter." That's all. No speech. A look across a courtyard. Peter remembers what Jesus told him, goes outside, and weeps bitterly. This wasn't Peter's first day as a disciple. He'd left his boats long before. And still, here, he turns again. Today's word is what happened in that look.
screen: `A COURTYARD, A FIRE.` → `THREE DENIALS.` → `THE LORD TURNING LOOKED ON PETER.`

segments.voice: The word is conversion. Mark's Gospel opens Jesus's preaching with it, in the Douay-Rheims: "The time is accomplished, and the kingdom of God is at hand: repent, and believe the gospel." The Catechism says that call comes first to people who don't yet know Christ, and that the first, deep conversion happens in baptism. But it doesn't end there. The Catechism speaks of a second conversion, and calls it an uninterrupted task for the whole Church, which, quoting the Second Vatican Council, it calls holy and always in need of purification. So conversion isn't a moment you get through once. It's a direction. And it isn't mainly a human effort. The Catechism calls it the movement of a contrite heart, drawn and moved by grace to answer God's merciful love. Then it gives Peter's story as the picture: after three denials, a look of infinite mercy draws tears of repentance from him. The prophets said it long before. Joel, in the Douay-Rheims: "rend your hearts, and not your garments." The Catechism says the call is first of all to an interior turning, not outward works like sackcloth and ashes, though without a change of heart those works would be empty, and with one they follow. It describes that turning as a reorientation of the whole life: away from evil, toward God, with real sorrow and the hope of mercy. And it's honest that the human heart is heavy and hard, so God has to give a new one. It quotes Lamentations: "Convert us, O Lord, to thee, and we shall be converted." Even the turning is a gift. Peter turned, and then kept turning, for the rest of the story.
screen: `REPENT, AND BELIEVE THE GOSPEL.` · `A SECOND CONVERSION, NEVER FINISHED.` · `REND YOUR HEARTS.` · `EVEN THE TURNING IS A GIFT.` · then, large: `CONVERT US, O LORD, TO THEE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: turn once today. Settle, and breathe. Let one small thing come to mind that's been pointing the wrong way. A habit of sharpness with one person. A lie you keep telling to make life easier. A grudge you're feeding. Don't make a list. Just one. Then picture yourself turning to face the other way, the way you'd turn your whole body toward someone who called your name. If you pray, you can ask God for that turn, with the words of Lamentations, or in silence. If you don't, just hold the image of turning. The bell holds the time.
Conversion. A turning of the whole heart toward God, begun in baptism, never finished, and itself a gift of grace. Today's word.
Your line: keep turning. Today, make the one turn you pictured, in one conversation or one choice, and then, if you slip, turn again. Day one thousand one hundred one.

howItsDone: Catholics speak of daily conversion and mark it in the examination of conscience, the penitential act at the start of Mass, Lent, and the sacrament of reconciliation.

fork.reveal: Peter remembered the word of the Lord, went out and wept bitterly. the Catechism calls that look one of infinite mercy.
